speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: asked	the Minister for National Development what is the recourse for HDB residents where there are repeated lift breakdowns, slow rectifications due to shortage of lift parts, lack of qualified manpower to conduct repair works and the lift company has already been penalised for slow rectification but still fails to deliver timely and effective service.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: asked	the Minister for National Development whether the recent spate of HDB lift malfunctions could have been prevented and whether there is an urgent need to step up the maintenance regime and audit checks to ensure high serviceability and safety standards of all lifts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: asked	the Minister for National Development whether the tightening of regulations for lift maintenance announced by BCA on 16 June 2016 takes into account the potential increase in demand for manpower in the relevant fields.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I understand and share the concerns raised by Members over the safety of our lift operations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Lifts are an integral part of our urbanised, high-rise living environment.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Currently, we have around 59,000 passenger lifts, with 24,000 of these in public housing estates, all of which are used with high-frequency on a daily basis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Lifts in Singapore are checked regularly and safe to operate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But like any other machinery, they can malfunction from time to time.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are perceptions that there had been a sudden surge in lift breakdowns.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is actual data from the Tele-Monitoring System (TMS), which all the Town Councils have.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is real-time monitoring data of HDB lifts operating in their respective estates.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have compiled the data and the breakdown rates were: 30 per 1,000 lifts in 2013 and 2014, on average.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And it has come down to 20 per 1,000 lifts per month in 2015 and the first half of this year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Nevertheless, despite the rates coming down, any serious lift incident is one too many.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Furthermore, as our lifts get older and are subject to more wear and tear, they will face higher risks of faults.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is why BCA, as the regulatory authority for lifts in Singapore, has been focusing on this issue for some time and it has been engaging the industry, consulting lift experts and studying international best practices and standards with the aim of enhancing the regulatory and safety regime for lifts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, let me share some of the key thrusts in our strategy and, in the process, also respond to the queries raised by Members.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our first priority is to raise our standards of lift maintenance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Currently, all lift owners, including Town Councils, have to engage a registered lift contractor to service the lifts at least once a month.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The lift contractors must also carry out an annual inspection and testing of the lifts, in the presence of an independent Authorised Examiner, who has to certify that such inspection and testing were done in accordance with regulatory standards and that the lifts are fit for operations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: While these monthly and annual checks are being carried out today, BCA's audits reveal that the quality of work can be improved.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is why BCA has recently announced measures to tighten maintenance standards for lifts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: BCA will also step up its audit checks to ensure that lift contractors achieve the required standards and to take enforcement action against non-compliance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, besides tighter regulatory requirements, it is also important for lift companies to build up their capabilities and have competent technicians and engineers doing the work.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: BCA is, therefore, working with the industry to set clearer requirements on the scope and level of training for all lift personnel.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is also developing a sectoral plan which will take into account the manpower demand in relevant fields of expertise, as well as the need for better defined career development pathways to attract and retain more skilled professionals in this sector.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Third, we should continue to effectively harness competitive forces in the industry to bring about benefits to residents.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are around eight main lift contractors that maintain about 70% of the lifts in Singapore, as well as many other smaller firms operating in the sector.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, there are many firms but eight larger ones that maintain about 70% of the lifts in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: All of these lift companies, big or small, are free to bid for the installation of lifts in our public housing estates.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: HDB adopts a stringent procurement process which takes into account not just cost, but also the quality and reliability of lifts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Lift companies that fail to meet this performance standard will be penalised, for example, through the imposition of 	Page: 16 liquidated damages or debarments for future HDB tenders.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Beyond this one-year DLP, Town Councils can decide whether to continue with the Original Equipment Manufacturer or switch to a third-party lift contractor.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, this will promote more effective competition and enable the Town Councils to choose the best contractor to do the job.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Fourth, besides regulatory action by BCA, it is also important for Town Councils, as lift owners, to take responsibility and carry out proactive maintenance and cyclical replacement of lifts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, Town Councils can analyse the lift fault data from the TMS and the records of residents' feedback to identify lifts in their estates which may require more attention.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Town Councils should also have qualified personnel within their management teams who can supervise the contractors and work with them to put in place an effective maintenance regime.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: A more comprehensive lift maintenance and replacement programme will cost more.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, with more rigorous checks over time, Town Councils are likely to draw more on their Sinking Funds to replace worn out lift parts or to carry out a complete replacement of older lifts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I had explained in this House earlier, HDB is already implementing the Selective Lift Replacement Programme (SLRP) to replace selected old lifts with new ones that come with better safety and security features on a cost-sharing basis with the Town Councils.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: To sum up, all of us, be it the Government, regulator, lift owners, contractors, or even lift users, have a part to play to ensure that our lifts are reliable and safe.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Over the years, we have put in place an effective operating and regulatory regime for lifts in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Would the Ministry consider rethinking how penalties are structured, as a nominal fee is hardly penalising and could also find its way back as higher maintenance charges that we have 	Page: 17 to pay lift contractors on a monthly basis?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will always review and make sure that our standards and our requirements are tight.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I would also highlight that Town Councils themselves have maintenance contracts with lift contractors, and Town Councils themselves can impose these tighter requirements on their own lift contractors which they engage to do maintenance work.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Minister mentioned the breakdown rate of 20 per 1,000 per month.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If you look at the HDB lifts that we have, it still represents about a few hundred a month.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It still appears high from a percentage standpoint.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I want to ask whether BCA sets a more stringent standard in terms of the breakdowns for all the HDB lifts.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The second question is: with the breakdowns that we have seen in the last few months, is there a need to review the procurement policies?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, whether the current contractual tenures for these lift maintenance contractors are too short for them, to the extent that they may not want to invest in lift maintenance capabilities because they are not sure whether they will still be in business after two years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, would we want to look into the tenure, as well as how they source the parts?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are still talks that maybe the parts that we sourced from a vendor that offers cheaper rates may compromise the quality.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, does that not require a review as well?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Twenty per 1,000 is still, I think, a figure that we should try to bring down even further.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That can only be done if we all work together, as I said.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There will not be a magic solution, but that can only be done if we tighten up across the board – procurement, maintenance and timely replacement.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I agree with the Member on his subsequent point that we should look at procurement standards as well, and we are.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I mentioned, we will look at making sure that our standards are tight, that we procure not just looking at cost, but also looking at quality, which includes looking at the source, the origins of where the various lift parts are made, as the Member had suggested.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It may mean a bit of a higher cost, but it also means that the Town Council is locked into the OEM for a longer period of time and you would not have the flexibility to allow competition to come in and to switch between different contractors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we have to find a balance, but we are prepared to consider a longer DLP.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Could I understand a little bit more about what was the reason for BCA reviewing this requirement for display and what role BCA will be taking, beyond just providing the issuance of the certificate?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Lastly – I think this is also an issue that many fellow Members have raised in their questions – with the more stringent inspection regime and possibly a lot more servicing required, is BCA aware of the manpower situation in the lift maintenance and lift manufacturing industry and whether we will be facing issues with lack of manpower in the short term?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First of all, on the findings of BCA's audits, I would say that across the various audits and also the investigation of incidents that have happened so far, BCA has not found any systemic trend, or identifiable trends across the various incidents.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Each one is quite unique, it varies across different lift models and different ages.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If you were to take a more preventive or risk-based approach, I would say, step up the maintenance and have preventive checks for the older lifts, particularly the ones which are above 20 years old.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is commonsense because these are lifts which have been subject to more wear and tear and, therefore, they need better maintenance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the Certificate of Lifts, the Member mentioned that it was taken away previously.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But even though there was not a requirement to display, the certificates continued to be lodged with BCA.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We want to make sure that it is not just about the certificate and the display of it, but to make sure that proper checks are done before the lifts are allowed to operate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Once that permit to operate is issued, it will be displayed, together with the Authorised Examiner's name, so that there is accountability – the person who did the checks, the name is there, is displayed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Potentially, even the lift contractor's name will be put up, together with the certificate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Third, on manpower requirements, we are mindful that this may require more people in the industry, in the immediate term.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In the longer term, we will, as I have said, look at sectoral plans to develop and ensure a healthy pipeline of technicians and engineers in this sector.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In the immediate term, we are still in discussion with all the lift contractors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: BCA is engaging them to identify specifically whether there are immediate manpower needs and how best to help them address these manpower needs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would just like to ask the Minister specifically with regard to lifts which are above 20 years of age ‒ which, the Minister has acknowledged ‒ tend to have more maintenance-related issues.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think the point of balance for Town Councils would be to enhance contracts and, by doing so, require more regular lift maintenance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That would mean increasing routine expenditure for the Town Council.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would have to be balanced against making a decision to replace the lifts or upgrade the lifts earlier.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That would, of course, entail the use of sinking funds.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, that is the real issue for many Town Councils, 	Page: 19 I believe.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In that light, with regard to the safety enhancements that the Minister has spoken about that HDB is looking at, and because it may cost a large sum of money, does the Minister have any estimate of when HDB will come to that decision?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Obviously, it would not make sense for us to spend a lot of money on safety enhancements on a lift that is already going to be due for replacement next year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because the better thing to do, as Mr Pritam Singh has suggested, is for the Town Councils to replace these very old lifts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, these safety enhancements would be done, as I had mentioned in my answer earlier, for lifts that are not due for replacement soon.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Exactly what age, we will have to study and this will take time to implement as well because we are talking about a huge stock of existing lifts which we will have to do progressively over a few years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I know that Town Councils need the data and the information to plan and we will strive to provide this information as soon as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister mentioned earlier that the breakdown rate actually improved by one-third.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: He also mentioned that the total number of lifts in operation right now is 59,000.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Does that actually imply that the number of lifts that have been brought into operation in recent years has outpaced the available supply of manpower that can handle the maintenance for such lifts?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I would say, if you take another measure and look at the number of technicians per lift we have and compare that against other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we have done some comparisons against Japan, for example.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We actually have more technicians per lift, compared to Japan.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is important to ensure that we have enough people, but it is also important to ensure that we have the people with the requisite skills and competencies and who are doing their jobs well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, as I have mentioned earlier, we are in the process of engaging the industry to understand better their manpower needs for the immediate term.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But in the long term, we do want to make sure that we have a good and healthy pipeline of people with the right skills and the right competencies coming into the sector and who are also continually upgrading their skills and keeping pace with new advances in lift technologies and safety.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, may I ask, currently, during the DLP, how 	Page: 20 much are the liquidated damages for poor lift maintenance for these newly-installed lifts?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Thirdly, under what circumstances would the lift company be barred from the next tender, given what I have just shared?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Lastly, I would like to ask the Minister again whether the Ministry will consider shortening the replacement period from 28 years to, perhaps, a period that is closer to the private sector's benchmark of 15 years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Can I just ask the Member in response?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am not aware that there is a private sector benchmark of a 15-year replacement for lifts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It sounds to me to be very, very short and I wonder where the Member got that figure from.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I asked the engineering team and, from what I was told, generally speaking, the lift replacement period is about 15 years, plus or minus.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Based on what I have come to understand, it is a shorter period of an average of about 15 years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As far as I am aware from BCA's checks with the industry, there is no such 15-year guideline in place across the board, certainly, for private sector lifts in Singapore or anywhere in the world, for that matter.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is from what we have gathered so far.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, if you look around the world, too, at lift replacement, it is a wide range.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It cannot be prescriptive because these are machines and the replacement guide will depend on your usage frequency and standard of maintenance over the years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Obviously, if it is well maintained, it may even go beyond 28 years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But if it is a lift that has not been well maintained in the past, then you may want to replace it even earlier.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Or, for that matter, you may want to replace most of the parts before 28 years are up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Replacement, really, has to be done on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Town Councils will, therefore, have to work with their lift contractors, looking at each particular lift, the model, the age, the history of maintenance, and then make a decision consciously whether to do early replacement or maybe to change some of the major parts or to allow the lift to continue with a good maintenance regime.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I have said, we are looking at clearer guidelines and training requirements for all lift personnel, including the technicians.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the second point about new lifts and the liquidated damages, I would say, we are aware that, for new lifts, there is generally also a higher breakdown rate or reported fault rate in the first year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And this is across the board, particularly because of teething issues or maybe, sometimes, it is related to residents moving in – renovation contractors and all sorts of things ̶ user habits.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The lift fault rate tends to stabilise after the first year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And, then, as I have said, with wear and tear, you start to see older lifts having higher fault rates as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But, first year, it is really a teething issue.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So long as it is within the DLP, HDB will work with the lift contractor to make sure that any of these teething issues with your new lifts in your new BTO flats are resolved expediently and as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, on that score, you do not have to worry that you will have a recalcitrant contractor bidding for another future contract.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I would say that most contractors that we have dealt with for these new lifts have been very responsive and they have come forward to make sure that whatever the complaints are for the new lifts, their issues are resolved as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Would the Minister consider asking the HDB to specify in the procurement specifications to ask the lift suppliers to supply a list of OEMs that can supply the major parts?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Second clarification: has the Competition Commission started to intervene and compel the lift companies to provide alternative sources of their lift parts?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am sure they would be putting up their findings soon.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I have said, the purpose of their investigation is to require OEMs to make available lift spare parts to all third-party contractors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, they will put up their findings on the lift sector and how they intend to put these in place.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the first point on open standards and procurement so that you have suppliers that would indicate which are the third-party contractors or how their parts can be supplied, I think the main thing is, if there is a contractor who comes in, installs a lift, what we would like to see is that the supplier of that new lift would make available the parts related to the lift to other third-party contractors, or other OEMs for that matter, so that whichever lift contractor the Town Council chooses for maintenance subsequently, the Town Council will not necessarily be held hostage to one contractor only.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is our intent and what we will strive to do in our procurement.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If BCA is able to identify such sentinel events, will it make the reporting and recording of such events mandatory?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is a rich database that allows Town Councils to already do data analytics to understand better which are the lifts with higher fault rates and, for those with higher fault rates, to go in, understand the reasons why this is happening and, if need be, take corrective actions, take remedial actions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have found out, for example, in some instances, it is due to the newspaper vendor coming in every morning and jamming the lift doors when they deliver newspapers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it may not be because of a mechanical problem.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But with that kind of data analytics, as the Member has suggested, I think lift owners should take the responsibility to make use of these data and improve the maintenance regime.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That applies across the board to all lift owners.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I welcome the recent tightening of the maintenance regime for lifts.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will HDB be more stringent in checking the lifts that are being installed in our new BTO projects?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For your information, this 	Page: 22 morning, I went and tried one new BTO lift which was just handed over recently but it was so noisy, no air, so hot inside and the HDB took over and gave it to the residents to use.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Because part of the problem is that a lot of downtime is due to trouble-shooting, which is inevitable when the lifts break down.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But when it has a lot of trial and error, I think that can be avoided.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why BCA has already been beefing up its experts team within BCA.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, they will also be setting up an experts panel to provide advisory and technical expertise, in particular.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will be strengthening this area within BCA and, if Town Councils or any lift owners, for that matter, would like to get technical advice, they can approach BCA for it.
